notes:
I've gathered verse-by-verse notes on Acts 24, but there are gaps. I ran out of searches and page reads before I could cover everything. The Enduring Word page I read stopped partway through v. 25, and the Precept Austin page only loaded through v. 2. I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, catholic.com, ligonier.org, the Lutheran or Pentecostal denominational sites, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so none of those appear below.

**Acts 24 – Research notes**

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the high priest, the elders and a trained lawyer all came to Felix's court, which shows how determined the Jewish leaders were to get a conviction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Precept Austin points out that the high priest Ananias was a Sadducee, the party most offended by Paul's teaching on the resurrection. It also says the Greek word for Tertullus means a public speaker or advocate, and is used only here in the New Testament. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-24-commentary
- Chrysostom (a Church Father read by both Orthodox and Catholics) says the leaders kept coming despite many obstacles, "only to be put to shame here also," and asks why they needed a hired speaker at all. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210150.htm
- Pulpit Commentary's opening principle: Hypocrites, when they can not do what they want to do by force and deceit, at length they go about to accomplish it by a show of law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-1.htm

**vv. 2–4**
- Guzik calls Tertullus's praise lies dressed up as flattery. Felix had brought neither peace nor prosperity, and Guzik quotes Stott that Felix put down revolts so brutally that the Jews felt horror, not thanks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Guzik also gives background: Felix was born a slave and rose through his brother Pallas, a friend of Emperor Claudius. Tacitus said he wielded a king's power "with the spirit of a slave." Guzik adds a short Bible study on flattery as a sin (Rom 16:18; Jude 16; Prov 20:19; Ps 78:36). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Matthew Poole notes that winning the judge's favour was a standard speaker's technique. Felix had cleared out some robber bands, but historians mostly remember him for greed and cruelty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-2.htm
- Bob Deffinbaugh (bible.org) quotes F. F. Bruce on Felix's career, his unusual rise from slavery and his three royal wives. https://bible.org/seriespage/divine-confinement-acts-241-27
- Chrysostom: the speaker praises the judge from the very start to win him over in advance. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210150.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary sums up the speech as three parts—flattery, falsehood, and misrepresentation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-24.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Tertullus tried to class Paul with the rebels against Rome. "Nazarene" was a mild insult, since Nazareth had a poor reputation (John 1:46). "All over the world" was an accidental compliment to how far Paul's work had spread. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Deffinbaugh: calling Paul a ringleader of a sect was meant to cut him off from mainstream Judaism, so he would lose the protection Rome gave to Jews. https://bible.org/seriespage/divine-confinement-acts-241-27
- Utley (bible.org) on "sect": the Greek word first meant a faction and later came to mean "heresy." In this context in Acts, Paul considers Christianity an integral part of the historical Jewish faith and hope. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-24
- Precept Austin quotes A. T. Robertson: stirring up revolt was a crime under Roman law, if it could be proved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-24-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik: this was the only specific charge, and Tertullus offered no evidence because there was none. It rested on rumour (Acts 21:26–29). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Utley notes that the charge in 21:28 was that Paul *had* defiled the temple; here it has shrunk to "tried to." https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-24
- Chrysostom: Tertullus says Paul "attempted" to profane the temple, but never says how. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210150.htm

**vv. 6b–8a (KJV v. 7): the textual question**
- NET Bible note: these words are missing from the oldest manuscripts (𝔓74, א, A, B and others). The note says they are most likely not a part of the original text of Acts, for not only is it lacking from the better witnesses, there is no easy explanation as to *how* such could be missing from them. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Act+24%3A7
- Precept Austin: probably a later insertion by someone other than Luke. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-24-commentary
- Utley: the added words appear in manuscript E (8th century) and later minuscules, and they shift the blame for violence from the Jewish leaders onto Lysias. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-24
- Catholic (Knox translation note on New Advent): some manuscripts lack parts of this passage. As the text stands, it isn't certain whether Felix is asked to question Paul or Lysias, but probably Paul. https://www.newadvent.org/bible/act024.htm
- Older commentators who read the longer text:
  - Gill (Baptist) says the leaders' real aim was not a legal trial but to kill Paul, as the zealots did. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-7.html
  - Matthew Henry says Lysias's force was no more than needed, and that he actually did the accusers a kindness by keeping them from guilt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-6.html
  - Calvin (Reformed) reads the complaint as a request that Felix give back to the Jews the right to judge the case, which Lysias had taken from them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-6.html

**vv. 8–9**
- Guzik: Tertullus didn't even pretend to have outside evidence; his only hope was that Paul would incriminate himself. Guzik quotes Clarke that few could have done better with so bad a case. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Dunagan suggests "examining him" may hint at torture by scourging. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-24.html
- Chrysostom: the same men acted as both accusers and witnesses. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210150.htm

**vv. 10–13**
- Guzik: Paul answered cheerfully because the facts were on his side, and notably used no flattery. Only twelve days had passed, so witnesses were easy to find, yet none were produced. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Clarke's verse 10 outline lists, among Paul's points, that he had kept a good conscience toward God and men. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/acts-24.html

**v. 14**
- Guzik: Paul had not left the God of his fathers or the Law and Prophets; he was fulfilling them. Tertullus says "sect"; Paul says "the Way." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Barnes: Paul shows he believed only what the Law and Prophets teach. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-14.html

**v. 15**
- Guzik: most devout Jews held this hope, though the Sadducees did not, and Paul tied it to Jesus' resurrection (1 Cor 15). Guzik adds a doctrinal point: a resurrection of the unjust as well as the just rules out soul-sleep or annihilation of the wicked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Matthew Henry: the just rise because of their union with Christ, the unjust because of Christ's rule over them as Judge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-16.html
- Light of Israel commentary quotes I. H. Marshall: this is the only passage where Paul plainly asserts the resurrection of all people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-14.html

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: because Paul took the resurrection seriously, his rule of life was to keep his conscience clear of deliberate sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-16.htm
- Barnes: a clear conscience needs two things: it must be properly informed about truth and duty, and what is known to be right must be faithfully done. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-16.htm
- Calvin (Reformed): conscience has two parts, an inner sense that looks to God alone, and the honesty toward people that flows from it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-16.html
- Thomas Manton (Puritan, on monergism.com): "void of offence" can mean that conscience is not wronged, or that we do not wrong others. Duties to God and to people must both be kept. https://www.monergism.com/sermons-upon-acts-2414-16-conscience
- Gill (Baptist): such a conscience is kept clean by being cleansed through Christ's blood. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-16.html
- Matthew Henry adds a caution: Paul had not reached perfection. "Always" means always free of *gross* offence; everyday weaknesses trouble the conscience but don't wound it the way deliberate sins do. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-16.html
- Coffman: conscience is not an infallible guide. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-16.html
- Contending for the Faith: a person can be sincere and sincerely wrong, so conscience must be trained by God's word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-16.html

**vv. 17–19**
- Guzik: the alms were the collection from the Gentile churches (Gal 2:10; Rom 15:26; 2 Cor 8–9). He quotes F. F. Bruce that the absence of the Asian Jews, who claimed to be eyewitnesses, was a strong point for Paul. Guzik's lesson: Christians shouldn't be timid about evidence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Barclay: the arrest came at the very moment Paul was bringing gifts for the poor and carefully keeping the Law, yet he defended himself without self-pity or bitterness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-26.html
- Chuck Smith: the people who saw him in the temple are the ones who should be there making accusations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-16.html
- Utley: the "if" in v. 19 is a Greek condition that expresses something very unlikely. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-24

**vv. 20–21**
- Guzik's treatment of vv. 14–21 is a single section; he presents the resurrection as the real point at issue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Deffinbaugh recalls the background in Acts 23, where Paul's cry about the resurrection split the Sanhedrin. https://bible.org/seriespage/divine-confinement-acts-241-27

**vv. 22–23**
- Guzik: waiting for Lysias was an excuse. Felix already had enough to rule for Paul, and the generous freedom he gave Paul shows he knew Paul was innocent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Precept Austin: Felix adjourned without a decision under a plausible pretext, that he required the presence of Lysias in person. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-24-commentary
- Chrysostom: governors often bent justice to avoid trouble with the Jews; Felix delayed not out of ignorance but because he knew the facts. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210151.htm
- bible.org: Felix knew more about Christianity than the religious leaders realised. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-24-28
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: there is no reason to think Lysias ever came. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-24.html

**v. 24**
- Guzik: Drusilla was the sister of Agrippa II and Bernice, about 20 years old. Felix lured her away from her husband and made her his third wife. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Wesley (Methodist): she left her husband Azizus, king of Emesa. She later died with her son in the eruption of Vesuvius. "The faith in Christ" means the doctrine of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/acts/24.htm
- Chrysostom thought it a mark of great honour that the governor's wife heard Paul too. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210151.htm

**v. 25**
- Ellicott: Paul's themes were exactly the weak points in the governor's armour. Felix's life showed no righteousness, and Drusilla beside him showed he had no self-control. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-25.htm
- Barnes: "self-control" (temperance) here points to the couple living in adultery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-25.htm
- Poole: Paul put the plaster where the sore was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-25.htm
- Guzik speculates that Paul's three points meant the righteousness we have in Christ, Christian ethics, and eternal accountability. He quotes Spurgeon that ministers must be personal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Constable and Deffinbaugh both link the three topics to the Spirit convicting the world of sin, righteousness and judgment (John 16:8–11). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-25.html and https://bible.org/seriespage/divine-confinement-acts-241-27
- Barnes: the Greek word means Felix was alarmed or terrified, not that his body shook. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/24-25.htm
- The standard reading is that putting it off is dangerous:
  - Matthew Henry: "the present season is, without doubt, the most convenient season." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_024.cfm
  - Guzik: delay is still rejection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
  - MacArthur (Grace to You, Baptist) uses the chapter to show the tragedy of postponing a decision about Christ. https://www.gty.org/sermons/1792/pauls-trial-before-felix-part-2-pauls-defense-begun
- **Where traditions differ in emphasis (why Felix trembled):**
  - Spurgeon (Calvinistic Baptist) puts it down to the Spirit's "restraining grace," which awakened Felix's conscience but does not save. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-25.html
  - Wesley (Methodist) stresses lost opportunity: the conviction could have ended "happily" had Felix followed it up, but the convenient season never came, and though he heard Paul again he was never terrified again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/acts/24.htm
- A dissenting older voice in the Biblical Illustrator argues that the usual harsh reading of Felix is unfair when a milder reading is just as natural, though it still presses hearers to decide today. https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/24-25.htm
- Catholic: the Douay-Rheims translation renders "self-control" as "chastity." https://biblehub.com/acts/24-25.htm
- Matthew Henry and Wesley both note that Drusilla did not tremble. Henry suggests she relied on keeping the ceremonial law to justify herself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-26.html

**v. 26**
- Calvin: Felix was ashamed to take Jewish money to condemn Paul, but as a greedy man he wouldn't free him for nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-26.html
- Clarke: greed joined to injustice; any fair judge would have freed Paul at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-26.html
- Chrysostom: "Observe his hardness of heart." Felix hoped for money from the very man preaching against it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210151.htm
- Guzik heads this section "greed": Felix, like Pilate, knew what was right and refused out of fear of man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-24/
- Bridgeway: Paul could have been freed if he had paid the bribe, but he refused. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-25.html
- Deffinbaugh: Felix's repeated hearing of the gospel only increased his judgment. https://bible.org/seriespage/divine-confinement-acts-241-27

**v. 27**
- Chrysostom: Felix wanted not just money but popularity. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210151.htm
- William Kelly: Felix was not short of sense or judgment, "and so much the worse for him"; he sacrificed justice for his own ends. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-25.html
- Deffinbaugh: readers expect a "not guilty" verdict, but Felix puts off a ruling and leaves Paul in prison for two years. https://bible.org/seriespage/divine-confinement-acts-241-27
- Contending for the Faith: Felix later fell from power and died in exile in Gaul, and Drusilla died in the Vesuvius eruption. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/24-25.html
